category: Lists & Arrays II: Sequences, Predicates & Array Operations
description: Second tier of list and array functionality: extremal selection, subsequence pattern matching, set predicates, padding and reshaping, array-level maps, scaling, and permutation utilities.

tools.name: MinMax
tools.description: Returns {min, max} of a list (or of all elements at any depth) in one pass. Use it for plot ranges, normalisation and data validation; an optional padding argument widens the range.

parameters.name: dx
parameters.description: Optional absolute padding, or Scaled[s] for relative padding.

tools.name: TakeLargest
tools.description: Gives the n largest elements of a list in decreasing order; for associations it keeps keys. Much faster than sorting the whole list when n is small. TakeSmallest, TakeLargestBy and TakeSmallestBy are the companions.

parameters.name: list
parameters.description: List or association of comparable elements.

tools.name: TakeLargestBy
tools.description: Gives the n elements of a list for which f[elem] is largest, in decreasing order of f. Use it to pick top-k records by a computed score without sorting everything. TakeSmallestBy is the mirror image.
tools.usage:
TakeLargestBy[list, f, n]
TakeSmallestBy[list, f, n]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Scoring function applied to each element.

tools.name: MaximalBy
tools.description: Returns all elements of a list for which f gives the maximal value (ties included). Use it instead of Sort/Last when you need every maximiser; MinimalBy is the mirror image. Both accept an optional count n.
tools.usage:
MaximalBy[list, f]
MaximalBy[list, f, n]
MinimalBy[list, f]

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Optional: return at most n elements.

tools.name: ReverseSort
tools.description: Sorts a list into decreasing canonical order; ReverseSortBy sorts by f in decreasing order. Cleaner and faster than Reverse[Sort[...]] and it handles associations.

tools.name: Subdivide
tools.description: Gives n+1 equally spaced values from xmin to xmax (default 0 to 1). It is the Wolfram equivalent of linspace and avoids the off-by-one errors of Range with a computed step.
tools.usage:
Subdivide[n]
Subdivide[xmax, n]
Subdivide[xmin, xmax, n]

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of subintervals (result has n+1 points).

tools.notes: Exact input gives exact rationals; use N or real endpoints for machine numbers.

tools.name: Subsequences
tools.description: Gives all contiguous subsequences (sublists) of a list, optionally restricted to lengths in nspec. Use it for n-gram generation, window enumeration and brute-force substring problems.

parameters.name: nspec
parameters.description: Length specification: n (up to n), {n} (exactly n), {nmin, nmax}.

tools.example:
Subsequences[{a, b, c}, {2}] (* {{a, b}, {b, c}} *)
Counts[Subsequences[Characters["banana"], {2}]]
tools.notes: Subsets gives non-contiguous combinations; Partition[list, n, 1] is faster for fixed-length sliding windows.

tools.name: SequenceCases
tools.description: Finds contiguous subsequences of a list that match a sequence pattern (using __, ___, Repeated, PatternSequence, Condition). It is the list analogue of StringCases and the right tool for run detection and motif search.
tools.usage:
SequenceCases[list, patt]
SequenceCases[list, patt -> rhs]
SequenceCases[list, patt, n]

parameters.name: patt
parameters.description: Sequence pattern such as {x_, y_} /; y > x or {1, ___, 1}.

parameters.name: Overlaps
parameters.description: Option: True/False/All to control overlapping matches.

tools.example:
SequenceCases[{1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 4}, {Repeated[2]}] (* {{2, 2}, {2, 2, 2}} *)
SequenceCases[data, {x_, y_} /; y > 2 x :> {x, y}, Overlaps -> True]
tools.notes: SequencePosition, SequenceReplace, SequenceSplit and SequenceCount are the companions.

tools.name: SequencePosition
tools.description: Gives {start, end} index pairs of contiguous subsequences matching a sequence pattern. Use it to locate runs, motifs or events in signals and token lists.
tools.example: SequencePosition[{a, b, a, b, c}, {a, b}] (* {{1, 2}, {3, 4}} *)

tools.name: SequenceReplace
tools.description: Replaces contiguous subsequences matching a pattern with a new sequence. It is the list analogue of StringReplace: use it for tokenisation clean-up, run-length encoding and event rewriting.

parameters.name: patt -> rhs
parameters.description: Sequence pattern and replacement (rhs may be a list, which is spliced).

tools.example:
SequenceReplace[{1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0}, {0, 0} -> z] (* {1, z, 1, z} *)
SequenceReplace[tokens, {"New", "York"} -> "New York"]

tools.name: SequenceSplit
tools.description: Splits a list at every subsequence matching a pattern, optionally keeping or transforming the delimiters. Use it for parsing token streams and segmenting signals at marker sequences.
tools.usage:
SequenceSplit[list, patt]
SequenceSplit[list, patt -> rhs]
SequenceSplit[list, {patt -> rhs, ...}, n]

parameters.name: rhs
parameters.description: Optional replacement inserted for each delimiter.

tools.name: SubsetCases
tools.description: Finds sublists of a list that match a pattern in any order (elements need not be contiguous), removing matched elements as it goes. Use it for combinatorial matching such as pairing complementary items. Companions: SubsetPosition, SubsetCount, SubsetReplace.
tools.usage:
SubsetCases[list, patt]
SubsetCases[list, patt -> rhs]
SubsetCases[list, patt, n]

parameters.name: patt
parameters.description: List pattern whose elements may match in any order, e.g. {x_, y_} /; x + y == 10.

tools.notes: Introduced in 12.1. Unlike SequenceCases, matches are unordered and non-contiguous.

tools.name: TakeDrop
tools.description: Splits a list into {Take[list, spec], Drop[list, spec]} in one call. Use it for head/tail splits, train/test partitions and cursor-style parsing.

parameters.name: spec
parameters.description: Same specification as Take: n, -n, {m, n}.

tools.name: TakeWhile
tools.description: Gives the longest prefix of a list whose elements all satisfy a predicate; LengthWhile gives just that prefix length. Use them for streaming-style parsing and to stop at the first failure without scanning the whole list.

tools.name: TakeList
tools.description: Splits a list into consecutive pieces of the given lengths, e.g. TakeList[list, {2, 3, All}]. Use it to unpack fixed-layout records and to chunk data by a length schedule; UpTo[n] tolerates short input.

parameters.name: {n1, n2, ...}
parameters.description: Lengths of successive pieces; All takes the remainder, UpTo[n] takes at most n.

tools.name: ContainsAll
tools.description: Tests whether list e1 contains every element of e2 (set semantics, ignoring order and multiplicity). ContainsAny, ContainsNone, ContainsExactly and ContainsOnly cover the other set relations; all accept SameTest and operator forms.
tools.usage:
ContainsAll[e1, e2]
ContainsAll[e2][e1]
ContainsAny[e1, e2]
ContainsNone[e1, e2]
ContainsExactly[e1, e2]
ContainsOnly[e1, e2]

parameters.name: e2
parameters.description: Elements that must / must not be present.

parameters.name: SameTest
parameters.description: Option: equivalence function used for comparison.

tools.example:
ContainsAll[{1, 2, 3, 4}, {2, 4}] (* True *)
Select[records, ContainsAny[{"urgent", "critical"}]@#["tags"] &]
ContainsOnly[{a, a, b}, {a, b}] (* True *)

tools.name: SubsetQ
tools.description: Yields True if list2 is a subset of list1 (every element of list2 occurs in list1). DisjointQ and IntersectingQ test for empty / non-empty intersection. These are the classic set predicates; ContainsAll is the newer operator-friendly form.
tools.usage:
SubsetQ[list1, list2]
DisjointQ[list1, list2]
IntersectingQ[list1, list2]

tools.name: DuplicateFreeQ
tools.description: Yields True if a list has no repeated elements (optionally under a custom equivalence test). Use it to validate keys and identifiers before building associations.
tools.example:
DuplicateFreeQ[{1, 2, 3}] (* True *)
DuplicateFreeQ[{"a", "A"}, ToLowerCase[#1] == ToLowerCase[#2] &] (* False *)

tools.name: CountDistinct
tools.description: Gives the number of distinct elements in a list; CountDistinctBy counts distinct values of f. Faster than Length[DeleteDuplicates[...]] and works on associations and Dataset columns.

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function whose distinct values are counted.

tools.example:
CountDistinct[{a, b, a, c}] (* 3 *)
CountDistinctBy[Range[20], Mod[#, 6] &] (* 6 *)

tools.name: AllTrue
tools.description: Yields True if test returns True for every element of a list; AnyTrue and NoneTrue are the existential and negated forms. Short-circuits on the first decisive element and has operator forms, making it the idiomatic replacement for And @@ Map[...].
tools.usage:
AllTrue[list, test]
AllTrue[test][list]
AnyTrue[list, test]
NoneTrue[list, test]
tools.example:
AllTrue[{2, 4, 6}, EvenQ] (* True *)
AnyTrue[data, MissingQ]
Select[matrices, AllTrue[Flatten[#], NumericQ] &]
tools.notes: AllMatch, AnyMatch and NoneMatch (13.x) are the pattern-based equivalents.

tools.name: Pick
tools.description: Selects the elements of list for which the corresponding element of a selector list matches True (or a given pattern). Use it for mask-based filtering, especially on packed arrays where it is much faster than Select.

parameters.name: patt
parameters.description: Pattern the selector elements must match (default True).

tools.example:
Pick[{a, b, c, d}, {True, False, True, False}] (* {a, c} *)
Pick[data, Map[# > 0 &, data]]
Pick[names, scores, _?(# > 90 &)]

tools.name: Catenate
tools.description: Concatenates a list of lists (or associations) into a single list, equivalent to Join @@ lists but faster and safer for large numbers of pieces. Use it to flatten exactly one level.

tools.name: PadLeft
tools.description: Pads a list on the left to length n with zeros or a given element (cyclic padding lists allowed); PadRight pads on the right. Both work on nested arrays with a list of lengths and can truncate. Use them to align sequences, build fixed-width records and zero-pad signals for FFT.
tools.usage:
PadLeft[list, n]
PadLeft[list, n, x]
PadLeft[list, {n1, n2}, x, m]
PadRight[list, n, x]

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Target length (or list of lengths per level).

parameters.name: m
parameters.description: Optional margin of padding to leave on the other side.

tools.name: ArrayPad
tools.description: Pads an array on all sides by m elements (or different amounts per side and dimension) with zeros, a constant, or modes such as "Fixed", "Periodic", "Reflected", "Reversed". Use it for convolution borders, image-like arrays and stencil computations; negative m crops.

parameters.name: m
parameters.description: Padding width (integer, per-dimension list or per-side pairs).

tools.name: ArrayDepth
tools.description: Gives the depth to which an expression is a full rectangular array (its tensor rank). Use it with ArrayQ, VectorQ and MatrixQ to validate input shapes before numerical routines.
tools.usage:
ArrayDepth[expr]
ArrayQ[expr]
ArrayQ[expr, d, test]
VectorQ[expr, test]

parameters.name: test
parameters.description: Predicate every element must satisfy, e.g. NumericQ.

tools.example:
ArrayDepth[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}] (* 2 *)
ArrayQ[data, 2, NumericQ]
VectorQ[{1, 2, x}, NumberQ] (* False *)

tools.name: BlockMap
tools.description: Applies f to non-overlapping (or overlapping, with an offset) blocks of length n of a list, i.e. Map over Partition without building the partition explicitly. Use it for block-wise reductions such as downsampling and windowed statistics.
tools.usage:
BlockMap[f, list, n]
BlockMap[f, list, n, d]
BlockMap[f, array, {n1, n2}]

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Block length (or list of block sizes per dimension).

tools.example:
BlockMap[Mean, Range[10], 2] (* {3/2, 7/2, 11/2, 15/2, 19/2} *)
BlockMap[Max, signal, 100, 50] (* overlapping windows *)
tools.notes: MovingMap is the time-series counterpart; ArrayFilter applies f to a neighbourhood around every element.

tools.name: ArrayFilter
tools.description: Applies f to the neighbourhood of radius r around every element of an array (edge handling via Padding), producing an array of the same shape. It is a general stencil / sliding-window operator for arbitrary functions, the generic version of MeanFilter or MedianFilter.
tools.usage:
ArrayFilter[f, array, r]
ArrayFilter[f, array, {r1, r2}]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function applied to each neighbourhood array.

parameters.name: Padding
parameters.description: Option: "Fixed", "Periodic", "Reflected", a value, or None (shrink output).

tools.name: ArrayComponents
tools.description: Replaces each distinct element of an array by an integer label (1, 2, ...), returning a same-shaped integer array; optionally a level and explicit label rules. Use it to turn categorical grids into index arrays for ArrayPlot, ComponentMeasurements or one-hot encoding.
tools.usage:
ArrayComponents[array]
ArrayComponents[array, level]
ArrayComponents[array, level, {elem1 -> id1, ...}]

parameters.name: level
parameters.description: Level at which elements are compared.

tools.name: ArrayRules
tools.description: Gives the list of position -> value rules for the nonzero (or non-default) elements of an array or SparseArray, ending with {_, _, ...} -> default. Use it to inspect or serialize sparse structure and to convert between dense and sparse representations.

parameters.name: val
parameters.description: Value to treat as the background (default 0).

tools.name: Rescale
tools.description: Linearly maps values from a source range (default MinMax of the data) to a target range (default {0, 1}). Use it for min-max normalization of features, mapping data to colour scales and unit-interval parameterisations.
tools.usage:
Rescale[list]
Rescale[x, {min, max}]
Rescale[x, {min, max}, {ymin, ymax}]

tools.name: Standardize
tools.description: Shifts and scales data to zero mean and unit standard deviation (z-scores); custom location and scale functions such as Median and InterquartileRange give robust variants. Standard preprocessing step before regression, clustering and PCA. Works column-wise on matrices.
tools.usage:
Standardize[list]
Standardize[list, f1]
Standardize[list, f1, f2]

tools.name: Threaded
tools.description: Wraps a list so that arithmetic and other listable operations thread it against the lowest level of a higher-rank array instead of the top level (NumPy-style broadcasting). Use it to add a row vector to every row of a matrix without Map or Transpose.

parameters.name: list
parameters.description: List to be broadcast along the innermost dimension.

tools.notes: Introduced in 13.1. Without Threaded, {{1,2},{3,4}} + {10,20} adds 10 to the first row and 20 to the second.

tools.name: Splice
tools.description: Splice[{e1, e2, ...}] inside a list splices the elements into the enclosing list, like Sequence but only within lists. It is the clean way to return several elements from a Map or replacement rule without Flatten.

parameters.name: h
parameters.description: Optional head into which splicing occurs (default List).

tools.notes: Introduced in 13.1; Nothing removes an element, Splice inserts several.

tools.name: SubsetMap
tools.description: Applies f to the elements at the given positions of a list, taken together as a list, and puts the results back in place. Use it to reorder, cumulate or jointly transform a subset of elements (e.g. Reverse the 2nd and 4th elements) in one step.

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function applied to the sublist of selected elements.

tools.example:
SubsetMap[Reverse, {a, b, c, d}, {2, 4}] (* {a, d, c, b} *)
SubsetMap[Accumulate, row, {1, 3, 5}]

tools.name: RotateRight
tools.description: Cyclically rotates the elements of a list n positions to the right (RotateLeft rotates left). Works at multiple levels for arrays. Use it for circular buffers, circulant matrices and periodic shifts of signals.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of positions (negative rotates left); list for multiple levels.

tools.example:
RotateRight[{1, 2, 3, 4}, 1] (* {4, 1, 2, 3} *)
Table[RotateRight[row, k], {k, 0, Length[row] - 1}] (* circulant matrix *)

tools.name: Permute
tools.description: Permutes the positions of the elements of an expression according to a permutation given in Cycles form or as a permutation list. Use it with FindPermutation, PermutationCycles and the group functions to apply symmetry operations to lists and arrays.

parameters.name: expr
parameters.description: List or expression whose elements are permuted.

parameters.name: perm
parameters.description: Cycles[{{i, j, ...}}] or a permutation list; a permutation group gives all images.

tools.example:
Permute[{a, b, c, d}, Cycles[{{1, 3}}]] (* {c, b, a, d} *)
Permute[{a, b, c}, {2, 3, 1}]
tools.notes: Part[list, perm] with a permutation list gathers elements, whereas Permute moves them; the two are inverses.

tools.name: RandomPermutation
tools.description: Generates a uniformly random permutation of n elements as a Cycles object (or several with RandomPermutation[n, m]). Use with Permute to shuffle, or RandomSample for a shuffled list directly.

tools.name: Cycles
tools.description: Represents a permutation as a product of disjoint cycles, the canonical permutation representation used by PermutationProduct, PermutationPower, InversePermutation, Permute and the group functions. PermutationCycles and PermutationList convert to and from list form.
tools.usage:
Cycles[{{a1, a2, ...}, {b1, b2, ...}, ...}]
PermutationCycles[permlist]
PermutationList[cyc]
PermutationList[cyc, n]

parameters.name: {a1, a2, ...}
parameters.description: Cycle mapping a1 -> a2 -> ... -> a1 (disjoint from the others).

tools.name: PermutationProduct
tools.description: Composes permutations (apply the first, then the second). PermutationPower raises a permutation to an integer power, InversePermutation inverts it, PermutationOrder gives its order and PermutationSupport the moved points. These form the basic arithmetic of the permutation group functions.
tools.usage:
PermutationProduct[p1, p2, ...]
PermutationPower[p, n]
InversePermutation[p]
PermutationOrder[p]
PermutationSupport[p]

parameters.name: p, p1, p2
parameters.description: Permutations in Cycles form (or permutation lists).

tools.notes: Products are applied left to right, which is the opposite of function composition order.

tools.name: FindPermutation
tools.description: Finds the permutation that maps one list to a rearranged version (or to its sorted form when a single argument is given). Use it to recover reorderings, e.g. how rows were sorted, and to apply the same reordering elsewhere with Permute.

parameters.name: expr2
parameters.description: Rearranged list with the same elements.

tools.example:
p = FindPermutation[{c, a, b}, {a, b, c}];
Permute[{c, a, b}, p] (* {a, b, c} *)

tools.name: Signature
tools.description: Gives the signature (+1 even, -1 odd, 0 if repeated elements) of the permutation needed to sort a list. Use it for determinant formulas, Levi-Civita symbols and parity checks.

parameters.name: list
parameters.description: List whose permutation parity relative to sorted order is computed.

tools.name: UnitVector
tools.description: Gives the n-dimensional unit vector with a 1 in position i (2D if n omitted). Use it for basis vectors, one-hot encodings and constructing matrices column by column.

tools.name: Ramp
tools.description: Gives x for x >= 0 and 0 otherwise (the ReLU function), listable and usable symbolically. Use it for rectification in signal processing, piecewise models and neural-network style activations.
tools.notes: Clip[x, {0, Infinity}] is equivalent; ElementwiseLayer[Ramp] gives a ReLU layer.

tools.name: BinCounts
tools.description: Counts how many data values fall into each bin of width dx (or specified bin boundaries); BinLists returns the values themselves grouped by bin. Use them for histogram data without plotting, and for multidimensional binning.
tools.usage:
BinCounts[data]
BinCounts[data, dx]
BinCounts[data, {xmin, xmax, dx}]
BinCounts[data, {{b1, b2, ...}}]
BinLists[data, dx]

parameters.name: dx
parameters.description: Bin width, or {xmin, xmax, dx}, or {{b1, b2, ...}} explicit boundaries.

tools.notes: HistogramList returns both bin boundaries and counts using Histogram's automatic binning.
